original_complete_all17_actual_punctuati.text: In the winter of 1636–37, Dutch merchants and brokers met in taverns to trade contracts for tulip bulbs still in the ground, a speculative business they called windhandel, "trading in the wind".

original_complete_all17_actual_punctuati.text: Prices of prized "broken" tulips, with streaked petals, soared.
In early February 1637, at a sale in Haarlem, the hub of the trade, no one would bid.
Days later, at an auction in Alkmaar, one bulb still fetched 5,200 guilders, the Dutch currency of the day, more than a decade's wages for a skilled craftsman.

original_complete_all17_actual_punctuati.text: Prices collapsed, many buyers defaulted, and unsettled contracts piled up.
Why the market turned so swiftly is still contested.

original_complete_all17_actual_punctuati.text: Two centuries later, Charles Mackay, a Scottish journalist, recounted the episode in a book on popular delusions, casting it as national hysteria.
